repo_notes.content: Write the public wiki in English for application developers and maintainers. Start each section with the reader's task or question, and link to the detailed child pages instead of repeating their configuration tables and procedures.

Ground claims in the indexed revision and cite files and symbols. Use README.md for supported workflows, zephyr/Kconfig for options and defaults, vendor/mrubyc/src/VERSION for version identifiers, and vendor/mrubyc/src/load.c for the accepted RITE format. Verify that examples agree with those sources.

Use consistent names: mruby/c is the firmware runtime, mruby supplies the host-side mrbc compiler, and mrubyc-zephyr packages the runtime for Zephyr. Use the upstream release documentation for broader context and the vendored sources for behavior in this revision.

Distinguish upstream mruby/c capabilities, modes exposed by this Zephyr integration, and configurations exercised by this repository's tests. Treat board support, Kconfig ranges, Ruby language compatibility, and test coverage as separate questions.

Identify the ownership boundary: vendor/mrubyc/src/ and zephyr/hal/ come from the upstream release. zephyr/Kconfig, zephyr/CMakeLists.txt, zephyr/fatal_hooks.h, cmake/, samples/, tests/, scripts/, and workflows are the integration surface.

Use source-linked diagrams where they clarify control or data flow. Show host versus firmware in the bytecode pipeline, the Zephyr thread versus Ruby tasks in the scheduler, and validation, CI, and approval in the release workflow.

For compatibility or security limitations, cite README.md and SECURITY.md. Describe the trusted-bytecode boundary, the impact on applications, and the private reporting path. Keep descriptions of security issues at the advisory and mitigation level.

Treat examples as revision-specific. Explain when a release tag in a west example must be available, distinguish board qualifiers in west build from platform names in Twister, and derive claims about CI, defaults, and released versions from their respective source or release records.

pages.title: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr
pages.purpose: Orient a reader choosing, installing, or embedding the module. Use README.md and point readers to the runtime, Zephyr integration, bytecode, and maintenance sections for implementation detail.

page_notes.content: Show the end-to-end flow from Ruby source to mrbc, the embedded C array, the application-owned memory pool, and Ruby tasks in a Zephyr thread.
Describe the repository map and identify the host build, firmware integration, and application responsibilities.
Offer two entry points: run the checked-in Hello sample first or add the module to an existing west application.

pages.title: What Is mruby/c?
pages.purpose: Explain the embedded runtime, the role of Ruby bytecode, and how mruby/c, mruby, and mrbc relate.
pages.parent: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr

page_notes.content: Explain why a firmware application can run Ruby using an embedded interpreter and a memory pool supplied by the application. Cite vendor/mrubyc/src/mrubyc.h and README.md.

Describe mruby as the upstream source of the host compiler mrbc and mruby/c as the separate runtime consuming compiled bytecode. Use the version metadata to explain why the tool and runtime versions both matter.

Use built-in classes and native C extensions as examples of the supported programming model. Refer to the embedded class library and compatibility pages for details of available methods and known limitations.

pages.title: Supported Targets and Toolchains
pages.purpose: Explain the supported Zephyr version, platform requirements, board identifiers, and host versus target build requirements.
pages.parent: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr

page_notes.content: Use west.yml, zephyr/Kconfig, and README.md for the Zephyr v3.7.2 LTS pin, CMSIS import, and 32-bit little-endian single-core gate with multithreading and a system clock.
Show what native_sim/native needs on a 64-bit Linux host and what qemu_cortex_m3 needs from the Arm toolchain, Zephyr SDK, and QEMU. Distinguish local west board syntax from Twister platform names.
Describe native_sim and qemu_cortex_m3 as the automated targets. Use the Kconfig gate to describe eligibility for other boards and the CI matrix to identify tested targets.

pages.title: Run Hello and the Task Scheduling Sample
pages.purpose: Walk through the checked-in samples from west initialization to the console output their Twister harnesses assert.
pages.parent: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr

page_notes.content: Use README.md for sample build and run commands. Verify options against each sample's CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf.

Trace samples/hello/hello.rb, its generated array, samples/hello/main.c, and the expected greeting followed by 'mruby/c finished'. Explain why building a checked-in sample requires no host bytecode generation.
Trace samples/vm_tasks/task_a.rb and task_b.rb. Explain the observed 'a:start', 'b:ran', 'a:done', and 'Scheduler returned 0' sequence using the Ruby sleep and the scheduler.

pages.title: Add the Module to a Zephyr Application
pages.purpose: Explain west manifest registration, local module discovery, and the application configuration required to use the runtime.
pages.parent: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr

page_notes.content: Show the README.md manifest project entry with a pinned revision and west update. For a local checkout, explain EXTRA_ZEPHYR_MODULES.
Trace zephyr/module.yml to the CMake and Kconfig entry points. Show CONFIG_MRUBYC=y and explain the roles of CONFIG_PRINTK and the system clock rate.
Separate module discovery errors from Kconfig dependency errors. Point readers to configuration and troubleshooting for how to inspect each.

pages.title: Initialize and Run Ruby from C
pages.purpose: Explain application ownership and the lifecycle from a bytecode array and aligned memory pool to the scheduler return.
pages.parent: Getting Started with mruby/c on Zephyr

page_notes.content: Use samples/hello/main.c and samples/vm_tasks/main.c for the order of mrbc_init, mrbc_create_task, and mrbc_run. Show the NULL return check on task creation.
Explain the required pool and bytecode storage lifetime, the need to size the pool and Zephyr thread stack separately, and why runtime calls remain on the designated Zephyr thread.
Show that mrbc_init also starts the HAL timer. Distinguish task creation, task completion, and returning from the scheduler using rrt0.c and README.md.

pages.title: Inside the mruby/c Runtime
pages.purpose: Map the vendored runtime from bytecode loading to dispatch, values, libraries, symbols, and allocation.

page_notes.content: Use vendor/mrubyc/src/mrubyc.h as the entry point and group source files by the work they perform.
Draw the flow from load.c to the IREP structures and VM registers, then to Ruby or C methods and the allocator.
Use vendor/mrubyc/src/VERSION to anchor behavior to the bundled release and link to the Zephyr port for platform-specific execution.

pages.title: Bytecode Loader and VM Dispatch
pages.purpose: Trace accepted bytecode into IREP structures and the register-based instruction dispatch loop.

page_notes.content: Use vendor/mrubyc/src/load.c and load.h to explain the RITE and IREP layers and what lives in the firmware byte array versus runtime state.
Use vendor/mrubyc/src/vm.h, vm.c, and opcode.h to explain register windows, call information, VM execution status, and how MRBC_SUPPORT_OP_EXT changes operand decoding.
Describe where exception state and the scheduler's preemption flag affect VM execution. Link to the format and known limitations pages for version matching and compatibility.

pages.title: Ruby Values, Numeric Types, and References
pages.purpose: Explain how mrbc_value represents immediate values and heap-backed objects, and why its C layout matters to extensions.

page_notes.content: Start with vendor/mrubyc/src/value.h, boxing_no.h, and value.c. Show the relationship between a value's type, its payload, and the mrbc_type or typed accessors.
Use c_numeric.c and the relevant Kconfig settings to explain the default integer width, the INT64 alternative, and single- versus double-precision Float.

Describe reference counting and pointer lifetime for heap-backed values. Refer to the C binding and configuration pages for argument ownership rules and the upstream representation alternatives that are outside the module's configuration.

pages.title: Built-in Classes and the Embedded Ruby Library
pages.purpose: Map Ruby features to the vendored C implementations, generated method tables, and mrblib.c.

page_notes.content: Use class.c, the c_*.c source files, and the _autogen_class_*.h tables to show how built-in classes and their method entries are registered.
Explain the role of the precompiled Ruby methods in vendor/mrubyc/src/mrblib.c alongside the C implementations. Link to the upstream release for the source of the Ruby library.

Map common questions about Array, Hash, String, Integer, Float, Range, Proc, and Math to their source. For String, distinguish byte indexing, optional UTF-8 indexing, and optional Unicode BMP case conversion.

pages.title: Symbols, Variables, and Method Lookup
pages.purpose: Explain the distinct uses of built-in symbols, runtime-interned symbols, lookup tables, and class or variable storage.

page_notes.content: Use symbol.c and _autogen_builtin_symbol.h to distinguish built-in symbol IDs from the dynamic symbol table and its configurable capacity.
Explain how MRBC_SYMBOL_SEARCH_LINEAR selects linear lookup and how the upstream default selects a binary tree. Cite symbol.c for lookup and existing tests for registration and reverse lookup.

Use class.c, global.c, and keyvalue.c to illustrate method lookup, constants and globals, and the capacity and growth of instance-variable storage. Distinguish these tables from the global symbol table.

pages.title: Memory Pool, Allocation, and Profiling
pages.purpose: Explain the application's pool, runtime allocation paths, memory accounting, and the available measurement APIs.

page_notes.content: Use alloc.c, alloc.h, and vm_config.h for pool initialization, the upstream MRBC_ALLOC_24BIT mode and its effective 32-bit size field with VM ID tracking disabled, and free-block size classes.
Distinguish instantaneous mrbc_alloc_statistics from optional profiling. Note that persistent allocations made at the pool tail appear in the next ordinary allocation or release sample.
Tie memory sizing to task/register and object demand, and explain the standard allocation-failure behavior. Send readers to the fatal policy page for Zephyr panic and optional statistics.

pages.title: Zephyr Integration and Configuration
pages.purpose: Describe how the runtime is built into a Zephyr image and where the application, scheduler, kernel, and HAL interact.

page_notes.content: Follow Zephyr module discovery through zephyr/module.yml to zephyr/Kconfig and zephyr/CMakeLists.txt and show where the official HAL is compiled.
Explain the shared MRUBYC_API interface for the runtime and application while identifying the fatal policy header as a runtime-only inclusion.
Guide readers to the C bindings, scheduler, HAL, configuration reference, or fatal policies depending on what they need to change.

pages.title: C Extensions and the Public API Contract
pages.purpose: Explain how a Zephyr library registers a Ruby-callable C method and shares the runtime's compile-time ABI.

page_notes.content: Use class.h, class.c, and value.h to describe mrbc_define_class, mrbc_define_method, mrbc_func_t, argument access, and returning a value. Ground ownership examples in real call sites.
Describe class layout and mrbc_define_destructor under MRBC_INSTANCE_DESTRUCTOR and the macro-controlled value, exception, and task layouts.

Show how APP_LINK_WITH_MRUBYC_API links the application automatically and how another Zephyr library uses zephyr_library_link_libraries(MRUBYC_API). Cite tests/mrubyc/main.c for compile-time agreement checks.

pages.title: Ruby Tasks and Scheduling
pages.purpose: Describe one Zephyr thread running multiple Ruby tasks, task queues, the scheduler loop, and sleep and join behavior.

page_notes.content: Use rrt0.h and rrt0.c to map dormant, ready, running, waiting, and suspended states, and show the role of the task control block and its VM.
Trace mrbc_tick, time-slice consumption, wakeups, mrbc_vm_run, and scheduler return or idle when tasks drain. Use samples/vm_tasks for a concrete scheduling example.
Explain that Ruby Task.create retains its VM when the task stops. Relate that lifecycle to joining and to the distinct fatal exception behavior.

pages.title: Zephyr HAL, Timer, and Console
pages.purpose: Trace the HAL from its Zephyr timer and nested critical sections to console output and abort.

page_notes.content: Use zephyr/hal/hal.c, hal.h, and rrt0.c to draw k_timer to mrbc_tick. Explain how the configured period interacts with the Zephyr system clock and delays.
Describe how nested IRQ locking takes a Zephyr scheduler lock outside ISR context and releases both locks at the outermost unwind. Explain the module's single-core assumptions from Kconfig.
Trace mrbc_hal_write through printk and mrubyc's CRLF path through console.c. Explain the UART console dependency and point to the fatal policy page for mrbc_hal_abort.

pages.title: Kconfig Defaults, Dependencies, and Fixed Modes
pages.purpose: Provide an exhaustive reference for this revision's Zephyr Kconfig declarations and the main upstream settings that are fixed or derived.

page_notes.content: Read every declaration in zephyr/Kconfig, including the module gate, the hidden application link symbol, and both Float alternatives. Give each prompt's Kconfig name, default, range or dependency, and resulting macro or action from zephyr/CMakeLists.txt and zephyr/fatal_hooks.h.

Group by VM capacities, language and class options, key-value storage, scheduler, and diagnostics. Compare with upstream defaults in vm_config.h and hal.h, including the module's choice to enable extended operands.

Use README.md and upstream sources to explain fixed, derived, or unavailable modes, including String and Float disablement, narrower integers, alternative allocators, NaN boxing, software ticks, and alignment. Mark generated tables and compiler flags where applicable.

pages.title: Out-of-Memory and Unhandled Exception Policies
pages.purpose: Explain both fatal hooks, their Kconfig controls, defaults, scope, and the scenario tests that support each claim.

page_notes.content: Trace MRBC_OUT_OF_MEMORY() from mrbc_raw_alloc to mrbc_hal_abort and k_panic. Describe how CONFIG_MRUBYC_OOM_POOL_STATS enables pool usage output and uses PRINTK.
Trace MRBC_ABORT_BY_EXCEPTION(vm) in mrbc_vm_end. Describe the default reporting and scheduler result, the opt-in Zephyr panic, and how rescue continues to handle ordinary Ruby exceptions.

Use rrt0.c and tests/fatal_hooks to explain why Ruby Task.create tasks skip the VM shutdown hook when they stop. Cover the test assertions for both OOM output modes, both exception policies, and the dynamic task.

pages.title: Bytecode Build and Compatibility
pages.purpose: Describe the contract from the host compiler to embedded RITE bytecode and organize the build and migration paths.

page_notes.content: Draw the Ruby source, host mrbc, generated header, compiler/linker, and firmware loader flow. Identify the interface checked at each step.
Distinguish checked-in sample headers from automatically generated application headers and show where to find the instructions for both.
Tie runtime or compiler upgrades to bytecode regeneration, a clean firmware build, and behavior checks for the exact application configuration.

pages.title: RITE Versions, Byte Order, and Alignment
pages.purpose: Explain the runtime's accepted RITE signature and how the loader reads encoded values on supported target architectures.

page_notes.content: Use vendor/mrubyc/src/load.c and cmake/mrubyc.cmake to explain the RITE0400 requirement for the current runtime and contrast the older RITE0300 fixture rejected by tests/mrubyc.
Use value.h, vm_config.h, and zephyr/CMakeLists.txt to distinguish little-endian targets from the requirements for safe reads of unaligned multibyte fields.

Describe the MRBC_REQUIRE_32BIT_ALIGNMENT rule for ARM Baseline or CONFIG_TRAP_UNALIGNED_ACCESS, the compiler option for strict traps, and upstream's 64-bit read policy. Use the Cortex-M3 trap scenario as evidence.

pages.title: Embed Ruby Scripts with CMake
pages.purpose: Document the mrubyc_embed_script application interface and how CMake generates, verifies, and publishes the C header.

page_notes.content: Show the helper included after find_package(Zephyr), an existing target, CONFIG_MRUBYC=y, an existing .rb path and a unique C symbol per target.
Explain the per-target output directory, compiler and source dependency tracking, and the temporary output renamed after the expected RITE prefix is verified.
Use cmake/mrubyc.cmake to explain host compiler discovery via PATH or an absolute MRUBYC_MRBC path. Distinguish version errors at configuration from script or output-signature errors at build time.

pages.title: Build and Pin the Host mrbc Compiler
pages.purpose: Explain where the pinned host compiler comes from, how it is verified, and what its header generation flags do.

page_notes.content: Read scripts/build-mrbc.sh and .github/actions/setup-mrbc/action.yml for the pinned source revision, checksum, build, and cache. Use vendor/mrubyc/src/VERSION to explain the exact compiler version expected by the helper.
Explain mrbc -B for a named C array and --remove-lv for omitting local variable name metadata. Headers may stay the same size when the input has no removable LVAR section.
Use scripts/check-bytecode.sh and the three sample headers to show how committed output is regenerated and checked. Link to the CMake page for generation inside an application build.

pages.title: Upgrade from v3.4.1 to v4.0.0
pages.purpose: Give a release-to-release checklist for the module, compiler, bytecode artifacts, C API changes, and rollback.

page_notes.content: Use README.md and vendor/mrubyc/src/VERSION to document the 3.4.1 and 4.0.0 module, compiler, and RITE pairs. Instruct readers to recompile every application script and clean-build the firmware after updating the west pin.
Point out the mrbc_find_method return type change identified in README.md and direct C binding authors to class.h for the current signature.
For rollback, restore the previous west pin, rebuild bytecode with its matching compiler, and repeat the clean firmware build. Link to known limitations to guide application-level regression checks.

pages.title: Runtime Compatibility and Trusted Bytecode
pages.purpose: Summarize the documented application compatibility limits of the bundled runtime and explain the trusted-input boundary.

page_notes.content: Use README.md for the known language behavior and recommend exercising application scripts with the pinned compiler and the same runtime settings. Avoid claiming full Ruby or upstream feature coverage from the success of one fixture.
Explain that matching the RITE version establishes a format contract. Only compile and embed bytecode from trusted sources, and refer readers to the advisory linked in README.md.
Use SECURITY.md for private reporting. Keep security guidance focused on applicable versions, impact, trusted input, and the reporting channel.

pages.title: Testing, CI, and Maintenance
pages.purpose: Guide maintainers through executable evidence, upstream synchronization, release automation, and diagnosis.

page_notes.content: Separate checked-in fixture tests, source and artifact verification, and GitHub workflow checks. Point each claim about support to the workflow or test that covers it.
Use a maintenance checklist from changing dependencies or the vendor bundle through local checks, CI, release validation, and post-release sample verification.
Provide links to the maintained workflow and script entry points so current pins, permissions, and job definitions govern future updates.

pages.title: Twister, Integration Tests, and POSIX Smoke
pages.purpose: Explain how to run the repository tests and what each automated scenario verifies.

page_notes.content: Use the sample.yaml files and tests/mrubyc/testcase.yaml to map sample output, defaults, custom configuration, OP_EXT, strict alignment, scheduler idle, and diagnostics to the platforms on which they run.

Describe the assertions that check Kconfig propagation, version rejection, pattern matching, timer behavior, and C extension behavior. Link to tests/fatal_hooks/testcase.yaml for the five console harness cases and their expectations.

Use scripts/posix-smoke.sh and tests/posix/main.c for the 32-bit host test against the official POSIX HAL. Distinguish this integration smoke test from the upstream Ruby test suite and physical-board testing.

pages.title: Vendor Provenance and Update Checks
pages.purpose: Describe the source-of-truth archive, generated upstream files, license handling, and the vendor update invariants.

page_notes.content: Use scripts/fetch-mrubyc.sh and scripts/check-vendor.sh for the release archive and SHA-256, then the byte-for-byte comparison of runtime, generated sources and headers, VERSION, licenses, and official Zephyr HAL.
Explain the upstream source-file exclusion list and compare the upstream Makefile's SRCS with zephyr_library_sources. Describe why an added upstream file requires a maintainer decision.

Give the order for a future update: check the upstream release and licenses, synchronize the files and source list, align mrbc and regenerate the headers, then run vendor, bytecode, and runtime checks.

pages.title: GitHub Actions, Caches, and Dependency Updates
pages.purpose: Explain the CI job matrix, cache boundaries, toolchain verification, and automated dependency maintenance.

page_notes.content: Use .github/workflows/ci.yml for the parallel board jobs and the separate bundled-source, POSIX smoke, and workflow-validation jobs. Describe what the Twister artifact contains for later diagnosis.

Trace the west project, SDK archive, compiler, and mrbc cache keys to their inputs. Use scripts/setup-zephyr-sdk.sh and .github/actions/setup-mrbc/action.yml for how pinned tools are installed and checked.
Use .github/dependabot.yml, .github/workflows/security.yml, and .github/workflows/scorecard.yml to explain update cadence and the distinct dependency, code, and repository checks.

pages.title: Release Tags and Production Approval
pages.purpose: Trace the tag-triggered GitHub Release from candidate commit and policy validation through shared CI and a production approval.

page_notes.content: Use .github/workflows/release.yml to explain why the tag must match MRUBYC_VERSION and point to a commit contained in main. Describe how the workflow checks production reviewers and the v* tag policy.
Show validation, reusable CI on the tagged source, and publication by a production-gated job with release-write permission. Use the workflow as the source for generated release note behavior.

Explain how to check the published tag, release page, and clean west sample build from the published revision. Use GitHub release records to distinguish an example tag from an existing published release.

pages.title: Troubleshoot Build and Runtime Problems
pages.purpose: Provide a symptom-driven path through module discovery, compiler checks, target constraints, scheduling, console output, and memory use.

page_notes.content: For a missing module or unavailable Kconfig option, check west list, zephyr/module.yml, the platform gate, and the build's resolved .config. For an embedding failure, check mrbc --version and the configured host executable.

For silent or duplicated output, check PRINTK, the console backend, UART CRLF, NO_STDIO, and the sample's expected output. For slow sleep, compare the configured mruby/c period with the Zephyr tick rate.

For memory or task failures, start with the aligned pool size, task creation result, scheduler return, and fatal hook output. Ask reporters for the module revision, Zephyr version, board, compiler version, and relevant Kconfig values.
